summary: Specifies how calendaring systems use iCalendar objects to interoperate for scheduling events, busy time, to-dos and journal entries. It is independent of the transport used to carry them. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 5546.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the set of polite messages calendars use to invite each other to meetings, accept, decline or suggest changes.

questions: how do calendars schedule meetings with each other
how do you accept or decline a meeting request
subtitle: A protocol for scheduling meetings and sharing calendar events between different calendar systems.

tldr.problem: Different calendar systems could not easily share meeting invitations, busy time information, or task assignments because they used different formats and methods to communicate scheduling changes.
tldr.mechanism: iTIP defines a standardized protocol for calendar systems to exchange iCalendar objects using common methods like REQUEST (to propose meetings), REPLY (to accept or decline), and COUNTER (to suggest changes), independent of how the messages are transported.
tldr.outcome: Calendar systems from different vendors could interoperate for basic group scheduling, though the protocol was replaced as calendar technology evolved.

facts.label: Number of methods
facts.value: 8 (PUBLISH, REQUEST, REPLY, ADD, CANCEL, REFRESH, COUNTER, DECLINECOUNTER)

today: RFC 2446 was replaced by RFC 5546 in 2009, which updated the specification for improved interoperability. The iTIP protocol remains the basis for calendar interoperability, though modern calendar systems use it in conjunction with additional standards like CalDAV.

sections.title: Calendar Interoperability
sections.content:
RFC 2446 defines iTIP (iCalendar Transport-Independent Interoperability Protocol), a protocol for calendar systems to schedule meetings, manage tasks, and exchange busy time information. It builds on the iCalendar data format (RFC 2445) and defines the scheduling semantics—the rules for who can send what messages and how the system should respond.

iTIP is transport-independent: the protocol defines what messages to exchange, but not how to deliver them. A separate binding document (like iMIP for email) specifies how to carry iTIP messages over a particular transport. This separation allows the same scheduling logic to work with email, HTTP, real-time protocols, or future transports.
sections.plainLanguage: iTIP is like a rulebook for how calendar programs talk to each other about meetings. It doesn't say how the messages get there (that is the job of a separate protocol)—just what polite things to say.

sections.title: Calendar Objects and Roles
sections.content:
iTIP messages are iCalendar objects with a METHOD property that specifies the message type. The protocol works with four types of calendar components: VEVENT (events), VTODO (tasks), VJOURNAL (journal entries), and VFREEBUSY (availability information).

iTIP defines two roles. An Organizer is a Calendar User (CU) who creates a calendar entry and sends scheduling messages. An Attendee is invited to attend the event or complete the task and responds with their status. For some messages, attendees can delegate to another person or suggest changes via the COUNTER method.

Calendar entries have state: the overall status is set by the Organizer, while each Attendee's status is tracked separately (NEEDS-ACTION, ACCEPTED, DECLINED, TENTATIVE, etc.). A sequence number ensures that the newest version of an entry supersedes older ones.
sections.plainLanguage: iTIP uses calendar cards like VEVENT (a meeting) or VTODO (a task). One person (the Organizer) sends the card and asks people to join. Others (Attendees) say yes, no, or maybe, and can ask to change the time.

sections.title: Scheduling Methods
sections.content:
iTIP defines eight scheduling methods, each with specific semantics:

PUBLISH: The Organizer publishes a calendar entry to one or more recipients with no expectation of response (like publishing a sports team's schedule). REQUEST: The Organizer asks Attendees to join an event or task; Attendees must respond. REPLY: Attendees send their status back to the Organizer. ADD: The Organizer adds instances to a recurring event or task. CANCEL: The Organizer cancels all or part of an entry. REFRESH: An Attendee asks for the latest version. COUNTER: An Attendee suggests changes (e.g., a different meeting time). DECLINECOUNTER: The Organizer rejects a counter-proposal.

Each method type has constraints on which calendar components it applies to. For example, REFRESH and COUNTER work with events and tasks but not journal entries or free/busy.
sections.plainLanguage: The Organizer can PUBLISH (announce), REQUEST (ask people), or CANCEL. Attendees can REPLY (say yes or no), COUNTER (suggest a change), or REFRESH (ask for updates). Each action is a different type of card to send.

sections.title: Handling Multiple Versions
sections.content:
Calendar entries can be updated many times. To handle out-of-order messages and conflicting versions, iTIP uses three keys: the UID (unique identifier) identifies the calendar entry, the SEQUENCE number tracks revisions (higher numbers override lower ones), and the DTSTAMP (date-time stamp) is a tiebreaker when UID and SEQUENCE match.

Attendees send REPLY messages to indicate their status relative to a particular revision. The Organizer tracks the highest SEQUENCE number in replies; replies with lower sequence numbers are considered responses to earlier versions. Rules also handle recurring events: the RECURRENCE-ID property identifies a single instance of a recurring component.

Implementations must persist UID, RECURRENCE-ID, SEQUENCE, and DTSTAMP for each component and attendee to correctly match incoming messages with stored entries.
sections.plainLanguage: When a meeting gets changed, everyone keeps track of the version number. If someone replies to an old version, the system knows not to count it. The program remembers important numbers (UID, SEQUENCE, date-time stamp) to keep things straight.

sections.title: Delegation and Acting on Behalf
sections.content:
An Attendee can delegate their attendance to another person. When delegating, the delegating Attendee sends a REQUEST method to the delegate and informs the Organizer using a REPLY with a DELEGATED-TO parameter pointing to the delegate.

Organizations often have one person managing schedules for another. iTIP supports this with a sent-by parameter in the ORGANIZER or ATTENDEE properties. When set, it indicates that the responding party is acting on behalf of the specified person. Additionally, an Attendee can have a descriptive role (e.g., "chair", "req-participant") separate from their organizational role.
sections.plainLanguage: If you can't go to a meeting, you can ask someone else to go for you. You tell the organizer who is going instead, and the organizer knows it is not you attending.

sections.title: Interoperability and Fallbacks
sections.content:
Not all calendar systems implement all iTIP features. The RFC defines fallback behaviors for partial implementations so systems can still interoperate even if one side lacks support for advanced features like recurring events or delegations.

Systems handle unexpected messages (e.g., a reply to an entry they do not know about) or late arrivals (an entry cancelled before the recipient gets the cancellation). Implementations should be lenient in accepting messages and strict about following the rules when sending.

Security threats include spoofing the organizer or attendees, eavesdropping on scheduling information, flooding a calendar with unwanted requests, and unauthorized changes. The RFC recommends using RFC 1847 to secure iTIP transactions (encryption and digital signatures) and implementing access controls to prevent unauthorized modifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Some calendar programs do not know all the fancy tricks (like repeating meetings). The rules say how a basic program should behave when talking to a fancy one. Security matters too: only trusted people should be able to change your calendar.
